newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia stocks extend fall despite support.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia stocks extend fall despite support.

text.p: Malaysian stocks were down at new 1-1/2 year lows at the halfway mark on Thursday with investors unimpressed by supportive comments from senior government officials, fund managers and dealers said.
At the market's midday break, the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's Composite Index was down 19.79 points, or 1.92 percent, at 1,013.45. The index plunged 2.32 percent on Wednesday.
The market last closed near that level on January 3, 1996, when it ended at 1,020.11 points.

Worries over rising domestic interest rates and possible ringgit volatility had added to the recent shifting out of funds to more attractive regional markets, and spillover from the Thai baht crisis and the Cambodian clashes, they said.
"People are scared to come into the market. With foreigners not in, it's difficult to go up," said an institutional dealer.
Bank Negara on Wednesday warned that it was willing to raise interest rates and even hinted at imposing capital controls to stamp out speculation in the ringgit.
"When there are fears that the central bank will come out to implement capital controls, the market will react negatively," said Kevin Chew, economist at Caspian Securities.
Verbal support of the market and the economy by both Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Government Economic Adviser Daim Zainuddin did not sway sentiment back into the positive.
Anwar, also the Finance Minister, said there was no reason to undermine the ringgit due to the country's stability and its strong economic fundamentals.
Daim, known widely as an astute stock market investor who is closely followed by retail players, said stock prices were low enough to buy.
"The market is so low it is an opportunity to buy," he told reporters at a fund management conference. "It is a time for you to buy," Daim added.
Said a fund manager at a Malaysian-based asset management firm: "The minute he said that, the market rebounded a few points. But we came down again."
Dealers said the market may come down some more in coming days if the outflow of foreign funds continues.
And stockbrokers and fund managers say the funds are not too keen on Kuala Lumpur presently.
"I think it's mainly because of divided attention in the region. A lot of foreigners are probably looking at Thailand, Indonesia," said Haizan Johari, investment manager at KL Mutual Fund.
A technical analyst said the Composite Index should find support at 1,000 points.
"Support is at 1,005 first, then 1,000. But oversold technicals may help to support the market," said Nizam Idris, technical analyst at research house I.D.E.A.
